title: I and You
hookLine: Martin Buber taught two ways of meeting the world: as an "it", or as a "you"
carry: every true you opens onto the eternal you
tomorrow: why would someone travel just to watch a rabbi tie his shoes?

lines: A BOOK ABOUT GOD... AND A TREE?
cards: At rehearsal, Noa's scene partner says every line to a spot just past her ear. Technically perfect. She feels like a lamp he happens to be standing near.

That's the answer to yesterday's question, and the philosopher Martin Buber built a small book around it. Say "it" to someone and they become something to use, sort or get past. Say "you" and something else starts.
Now the puzzle. Buber's book, I and Thou, is about God. So why does it stop, early on, to look hard at a tree?

teach.b: Start with Buber's claim. There are two basic words, and each is a pair: I-It and I-You. There's no I standing alone.
The I who measures and uses is a different I from the one who meets. Buber doesn't call It evil.
He says nobody can live without it; we need schedules, tools and facts. But a person who lives with It alone, he says, isn't fully human.

teach.h: EVEN A TREE CAN BE A YOU.
teach.b: Now the tree. Buber says he can look at a tree as a picture, a type of plant, a set of laws about water and light. All true, all It.
And yet, he writes, it can happen that he's drawn into relation with that tree, and it's no longer an object. It's a You. That's the puzzle solved.
The You isn't saved for God or for great loves. It's a way of meeting anything, starting with whatever's nearest.

teach.h: EVERY YOU OPENS ON THE ETERNAL YOU.
teach.b: And then Buber's turn: every You we meet is a glimpse through to what he calls the eternal You.

teach.h: EVERY TRUE YOU OPENS ONTO THE ETERNAL YOU.
teach.b: A book about God opens on a tree because, for Buber, that's where the road to God begins.
One fact to tell a friend: his German word was Du, the word for someone close, which is why some translators prefer "you" to the stiff old "thou".

how: Buber's I and Thou is read in Jewish adult study, in university courses and by readers of many faiths; his language of I-It and I-You is often used in teaching about prayer, marriage and friendship.

o: agreeing with someone so the two of you stay close
speaking politely and formally to people you respect
meeting someone as a whole person, not a thing to use

games.q: Buber's two words — tap the pairs.
p: can be an object, or a You

s: Buber says the I-It way is wrong and should be dropped
he says nobody can live without It; living with It alone is the problem.
in Buber's book, even a tree can be met as a You
he describes being drawn into relation with a tree.
Buber's German word for you was the formal, distant one

games.q: your mom asks how the new coworker is. you realize all you know is his job title and that he's slow on email. what would Buber point at?
o: so far he's only been an It: a role and a speed. meet him once.
that's normal at work; I-You is only for family and God.
you should avoid I-It thinking entirely, even at work.
games.why: Buber says we all need It, but anyone, even a tree, can become a You. the coworker hasn't been met yet.

practice: Pick up your phone and choose one person you'll see this week. Write them a single line that's only about them: not a plan, not a favor, just something you've noticed and like. Send it, or save it for when you see them.

wordCard.voice: Meet the you: Martin Buber's teaching that we can treat the world as It, to use, or meet it as You, whole and present.

orig.note: Hebrew: you (to one man). Buber's book in Hebrew is called Ani ve-Atah, I and You.

carryVoice: Here's the line: every true you opens onto the eternal you. For Buber, the road to God starts with whoever's nearest.
